fields.abstract: MUSS combines DNA-sequence embeddings with paired single-cell chromatin-accessibility and expression data to predict regulatory relationships and cell-specific expression, including for held-out genes and regions.

sections.title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
sections.subtitle: Biomedical & translational medicine; Quantitative methods.

fields.abstract: A primary-care EHR model's colorectal-cancer discrimination improved as the lookback period expanded to 18 years, then plateaued, with the authors finding a similar peak AUROC for XGBoost.
fields.authors: Achille Raviez, Lan Wang, Brendan Delaney.
fields.arxiv: 2611.07265v1 (published 2026-11-05 00:34:47 UTC; categories: cs.LG primary, cs.AI, q-bio.QM cross-lists).
fields.evidence for ranking: Semantic Scholar showed 0 citations and 0 influential citations. The arXiv comment identifies acceptance to the ML4H 2026 Findings Track. Inclusion is based on biomedical relevance and the long longitudinal evaluation, not measured popularity.
fields.claimed contribution: The authors pretrained on 1.4 billion coded events from 3.6 million North West London primary-care patients and evaluated 1,008 cases with 9,582 matched controls across 15 lookback windows; AUROC rose from 0.551 at two years to 0.590 at 18 years.
fields.caveat: The frozen evaluation cohort is from one health system, discrimination remains modest, and the study does not establish clinical utility, calibration, or prospective benefit. This is not a clinical screening recommendation.

sections.title: Resampling-based batch reweighting for ComBat harmonization of MRI radiomic features in a multi-scanner glioma cohort
sections.subtitle: Medical physics & imaging; Biomedical & translational medicine

fields.abstract: This revised study tests whether resampling underrepresented scanner batches before ComBat harmonization reduces residual scanner effects in MRI radiomic features while retaining tumor-grade information.
fields.authors: Rifa Sajda Tasnim, Yushuf Sharker, Md Forhad Hossain, Rakibur Rahman, Enamul Hoque Bhuiyan.
fields.arxiv: 2611.02156v2 (latest revision 2026-11-05 13:40:38 UTC; first submitted 2026-11-01 19:43:22 UTC; categories: eess.IV primary, physics.med-ph cross-list).
fields.evidence for ranking: Version 2 was announced in this batch; the arXiv comment says the manuscript was submitted to the Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging, not accepted. Included for its direct glioma-imaging application and cohort-based comparison.
fields.claimed contribution: In 733 patients from one center and nine vendor/field-strength batches, batch-augmented ComBat reduced features with significant residual scanner association from 13/428 to 8/428 compared with standard ComBat; the authors call the evidence exploratory with confirmatory tests.
fields.caveat: Retrospective, single-center data and imbalanced scanner batches limit transportability. Reduced scanner association alone does not prove preservation of all clinically relevant signal or improved patient outcomes.
fields.themes: Medical physics & imaging; Biomedical & translational medicine; Quantitative methods.

sections.title: Leveraging deep generative modelling at the agent level in discrete-event simulations
sections.subtitle: Biomedical & translational medicine; Quantitative methods.

fields.abstract: A conditional generative emulator replaces one component of a multi-disease agent-based simulation, reducing runtime while approximately recovering the modeled disability-adjusted-life-year trajectory.
fields.authors: Margherita Molaro, Matthew M. Graham, Oliver Watson, Rachel E. Murray-Watson, Martin Chalkley, Joseph H. Collins, Bingling She, Asif U. Tamuri, Timothy B. Hallett.
fields.arxiv: 2611.07995v1 (published 2026-11-05 13:23:39 UTC; categories: q-bio.QM primary, q-bio.PE cross-list).
fields.evidence for ranking: The arXiv comment says accepted for publication by the Journal of the Royal Society Interface. The authors report an 86.6% runtime reduction with a bootstrap interval and recovery of the cause-specific mean outcome within 13%; these are model-method results, not external attention measures.
fields.claimed contribution: The authors replace the road-traffic-injury component of Thanzi La Onse with a conditional tabular GAN while retaining the full multi-disease simulation framework.
fields.caveat: The demonstration concerns one modeled cause with low assumed fatal incidence and one simulation framework. It validates computational approximation, not real-world disease-burden estimates or public-health interventions.

sections.title: Trending Research Themes
sections.summary:
The clearest cluster is computational molecular discovery and evaluation: PharmAgents2 reports three experimentally followed drug-discovery scenarios, BILBY tests static protein-motif designs against molecular-dynamics behavior, and the DiffDock study finds that geometrically focused post-training did not consistently improve returned-pose success. These are distinct contributions and evidence types, not independent validations of a common system; only PharmAgents2 reports wet-lab follow-up, while BILBY and DiffDock are computational evaluations.

A second thread is representation and measurement in biomedical data. MUSS aligns sequence-derived representations with single-cell assays; the EHR study varies calendar lookback; and ComBat, SAGE, and CT studies examine scanner or acquisition effects. These papers use different datasets and endpoints, so this sample does not establish a field-wide shift.

A third, smaller group develops mechanistic or computational models: the K-channel paper derives kinetic reductions, reaction-network identification uses a frequency-domain approximation, and the disease-simulation paper accelerates one component of a multi-disease agent-based model. Each remains conditional on its model assumptions and validation setting.

sections.title: Open Problems and Research Directions
sections.summary:
- **Connect computational design success to orthogonal experiments.** PharmAgents2's selected wet-lab scenarios could be followed by preregistered, blinded studies across targets and assay types, with external laboratories and accounting for failed proposals. For BILBY and DiffDock, prospective assays and structural comparisons would test whether MD or docking criteria predict physical function.
- **Test biological and clinical portability.** MUSS needs independent cell types, assay platforms, and perturbation datasets; CRISPR perturbations could separate predictive enhancer–gene associations from causal regulation. The EHR result would benefit from external health-system validation, calibration, decision-utility analysis, and prospective evaluation; its modest AUROC should remain explicit.
- **Validate medical measurements across settings.** ComBat could be tested on multi-center cohorts with scanner/vendor holdouts and explicit checks for preserved grade/outcome signal. SAGE needs tissue-mimicking or in-vivo tests with known source locations and varying source density; CT reconstruction/dose relationships need multi-scanner and diagnostic-task studies. These are proposed follow-ups, not clinical advice.
- **Stress-test model-based simulations.** The agent-level disease simulator, reaction-network inference, K-channel kinetics, and biomedical-flow solver could be compared with independent datasets and measured parameter ranges, including sensitivity to assumptions and failure cases. These would test whether computational speed or explanatory fit transfers beyond the showcased examples.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.summary: The batch is strongest in computational molecular-design evaluation, with additional single-cell, longitudinal EHR, and medical-physics methods. PharmAgents2 reports limited wet-lab follow-up; most other selected results are computational, retrospective, simulated, or phantom-based. Citation evidence was sparse at the snapshot, so this is a relevance-ranked reading list—not a claim these were the most-read or most-popular papers.
